title: Mergers and Acquisitions (M&A): How Deals Affect Stock Prices
content:
Corporate mergers and acquisitions (M&A) are major corporate events that reshape competitive landscapes and drive sharp price movements in the shares of participating companies.

An acquisition occurs when one company (the acquirer) purchases a majority or complete stake in another company (the target). A merger occurs when two separate entities combine to form an entirely new joint operating business. Deals can be structured as all-cash transactions, stock-for-stock swaps, or a blend of both.

When an acquisition is announced, the target company's stock price typically jumps near the agreed buyout price. To incentivize shareholders to approve the sale, acquirers pay an acquisition premium—often 20% to 50% above the target company's pre-announcement market price. Conversely, the acquiring company's stock price frequently dips upon announcement, reflecting the heavy debt load, share dilution, or integration execution risks associated with the transaction.

The gap between the target's current trading price and the official acquisition offer is called the 'arbitrage spread.' This spread reflects the market's assessment of whether the transaction will close successfully. Major deals often face regulatory scrutiny from antitrust authorities, such as the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) or European Commission, who can block transactions that harm consumer competition. Investors holding shares of acquired companies should review the tax implications of receiving cash payouts versus stock compensation.
